posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the compliance pain around unexplainable AI outputs, add the insight that auditability is the real unlock, not accuracy
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' problem is basically the new 'the spreadsheet said so' — except the spreadsheet at least had a cell you could click into. What kills AI adoption in regulated industries isn't wrong answers, it's answers with no paper trail. Accuracy without auditability is just a liability dressed up as a feature.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person consultancy describing the exact trust gap Milo is built around — validate the pain with a specific observation, add the insight that the problem is credibility not the tool
posts.draft_comment: The dashboard was never the hard part. The moment someone spots one wrong number in a board meeting, the whole thing gets written off — and Excel feels 'safer' because everyone already knows its flaws. It's not really a Power BI problem, it's a trust problem. And you can't sprint your way out of that.

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post about dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why people stop trusting dashboards' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is actually pretty common — I've seen ops teams hit 60+ before someone finally asks 'wait, which one do we act on?' The usage jump makes complete sense. When a dashboard can't tell you what to do next, it stops feeling like a tool and starts feeling like homework. The real question is who owned those 42 metrics you cut, and how hard was that conversation?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging on self-service BI failure — validate the 'who owns truth' pain, add the insight that the problem isn't access it's definition, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so consistent it's almost a law. You don't have a tooling problem, you have a 'nobody agreed on revenue before you hit deploy' problem — and Power BI just made that visible faster. Most companies skip the unglamorous bit: locking down definitions before anyone touches a dashboard. Who's actually responsible for that in your org — data team, finance, or does it just fall into the void?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO framing AI hallucinations as a security risk, with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the reframe, add the trust layer insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The 'user input' comparison is the right framing and most analytics teams haven't caught up to it yet. We obsess over who can access data but barely question whether the output itself is trustworthy. A hallucinated number that looks clean and formatted is scarier than a permission error — at least the error throws a flag. How many orgs even have a process for auditing what the AI actually generated before it hits a deck?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with a post about BI tools failing non-technical users — validate the systemic problem with a specific observation, add depth without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The £200k is almost never the real cost. It's the six months of 'can you just pull that for me' requests that pile up on whoever built the thing, because everyone else quietly gave up trying. Most BI tools are essentially dashboards for people who could have written the SQL anyway. Wonder how many of those platforms even got opened in month three.

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market industrial company names a real data governance pain — validate the culture diagnosis and add the layer most people skip over
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, one dataset, three answers — that's not a filter problem, that's a trust problem. And the brutal thing is once your CFO loses faith in the dashboard, no amount of clean data gets it back quickly. Culture is the right call, but I'd add one thing: someone has to own the number. Not the tool, not the team — one person who says 'this is the version we present'. Does that role even exist at most companies?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing a real adoption failure with AI tools — validate the 'nobody knows what to ask' insight and reframe shadow AI as a signal worth paying attention to, not a compliance problem
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number is brutal but honestly not surprising. The 'what do I even ask it?' problem is the whole ballgame — most tools assume people already know what they don't know, which is kind of the whole reason they needed help in the first place. And yeah, the shadow AI thing is the part most IT leaders are treating as a security issue when really it's just people voting with their thumbs on what's actually useful to them.
